title: Primary Function of the Suspended Support System
learningObjectives: Connect the real suspended system to its structural load-transfer function.
student: What is the primary structural function of the suspended equipment support system?
instructor: The system supports a suspended equipment pod and transfers its weight through two inclined steel cables into wall-mounted anchor brackets and then into the building structure.
gradingNotes: Good answers should mention support of the pod, weight transfer, cables, wall anchors, and building structure.

title: External Load and Weight
learningObjectives: Identify the payload weight and where it acts in the idealized model.
student: Where is the external load applied, and what physical quantity creates it?
instructor: The external load is the equipment weight applied downward at the lower ring or connector B. The load is W = mg. For m = {{m}} {{m_unit}} and g = {{g}} {{g_unit}}, W = {{cable_weight_N}} N.
commonMistakes: Students sometimes place the pod weight at A or C. It acts at the payload/lower connector B.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Identify support idealizations for a cable-supported particle-equilibrium model.
student: Identify the supports or boundary constraints in the real system.
instructor: The wall-mounted brackets at A and C support the cables. In the idealized model, A and C are fixed anchor locations that provide cable reaction forces along the cable directions. The lower point B is a ring or shackle connection where the two cable forces and the payload weight meet.
gradingNotes: The most important free-body diagram is the lower joint B, not the entire wall frame.

title: Load Path to the Building Structure
learningObjectives: Trace the load path from payload to support structure.
student: Using the component list, trace the load path from the equipment pod to the building structure.
instructor: Equipment pod weight → lower ring/shackle at B → tension in cable AB and cable BC → wall anchors A and C → structural columns or walls → building frame/foundation.

title: Critical Components
learningObjectives: Identify which members are checked in the base mechanics problem.
student: Using the load path, identify the components most likely to be critical for this problem.
instructor: The critical components are the two steel cables AB and BC because they carry the payload through axial tension. The lower ring and wall anchor brackets are also part of the load path, but connector dimensions are not provided for a detailed connector stress check in the base problem.

title: Critical Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Choose the relevant mechanics response and reject irrelevant checks for the base model.
student: For each critical component, identify the relevant mechanical response or failure mechanism and rank them by importance.
instructor: The most important response is axial tensile stress in the cables. Secondary connector shear or bearing could be checked only if shackle, pin, bolt, or bracket dimensions are supplied. Buckling is not relevant because cables are tension-only members, and cable bending is neglected in this base model.

title: Relevant Geometry and Material Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the variables controlling cable tension, stress, and FOS.
student: Identify the geometric and material parameters that control the cable stress and factor of safety.
instructor: Relevant parameters include cable angles θAB = {{theta_AB}} {{theta_AB_unit}} and θBC = {{theta_BC}} {{theta_BC_unit}}, mass m, gravitational acceleration g, cable diameters dAB and dBC, cable cross-sectional areas AAB and ABC, cable failure stress σfail, and required factor of safety.

title: Student-Generated Cable Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the real suspended system into a 2D particle-equilibrium model.
imageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of the two-cable suspended equipment system
student: Convert the real system into a simplified 2D Mechanics of Materials model. The model should show support points A and C, lower joint B, cable members AB and BC, cable angles, the downward load W = mg, and the unknown cable tensions.
instructor: A correct idealization is a 2D particle-equilibrium model of joint B with two cable tensions directed away from B along cables BA and BC and a downward weight W. The cables are idealized as two-force tension members.
gradingNotes: This should be completed before students rely on the instructor reference diagram, unless the activity is intentionally scaffolded.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions needed for the simplified equilibrium and stress model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real support system into the simplified mechanics model.
instructor: The equipment pod is modeled as a point load at B; cable self-weight is neglected; each cable is straight and massless; each cable is a two-force tension member; loading is static; anchor locations are fixed; material behavior is represented only by failure stress; and connector flexibility, bracket stresses, fatigue, and installation tolerances are neglected.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the solution sequence from equilibrium to design recommendation.
student: Before calculating, describe the sequence of analysis required to evaluate the cables.
instructor: Draw the FBD of joint B; write equilibrium in x and y; solve for TAB and TBC; compute cable area from selected diameter or required area from allowable stress; compute σ = T/A; compute FOS = σfail/σ; and make an engineering recommendation.

title: Boundary Conditions from the Instructor Diagram
learningObjectives: Interpret the support and cable-force idealizations from the instructor diagram.
student: From the instructor reference diagram, identify the boundary conditions and support idealizations.
instructor: Points A and C are fixed wall anchor locations. The cables are attached to these supports and carry only tensile force along their own axes. Joint B is treated as a pin/ring where the two cable tensions and the downward weight act concurrently.
commonMistakes: This is not a beam support problem; do not introduce moment reactions at B.

title: Unknown Cable Forces
learningObjectives: Identify the two unknown member forces before writing equilibrium equations.
student: Identify the unknown forces that must be solved before the cable stresses can be evaluated.
instructor: The unknowns are the two cable tensions TAB and TBC. These are the force magnitudes transmitted by cables AB and BC. At joint B, each tension acts along its cable direction away from B.

title: Equilibrium Equations at Joint B
learningObjectives: Write 2D equilibrium equations for an asymmetric cable joint.
student: Draw the free-body diagram of joint B and write the x- and y-equilibrium equations.
instructor:
Using +x to the right and +y upward:

ΣFx = -TAB cos({{theta_AB}}°) + TBC cos({{theta_BC}}°) = 0.

ΣFy = TAB sin({{theta_AB}}°) + TBC sin({{theta_BC}}°) - W = 0.
commonMistakes: A common error is switching sine and cosine because the angles are measured from the horizontal.

title: Cable Tensions
learningObjectives: Solve the two equilibrium equations for cable tensions.
student: Using m = {{m}} kg and g = {{g}} m/s2, solve for TAB and TBC.
instructor: W = mg = {{cable_weight_N}} N. From horizontal equilibrium, TAB cos({{theta_AB}}°) = TBC cos({{theta_BC}}°). Solving with vertical equilibrium gives TAB = {{cable_T_AB_N}} N and TBC = {{cable_T_BC_N}} N. The larger cable tension is in {{cable_governing_tension_member}}.
gradingNotes: For the default geometry, cable AB carries the larger tension because the angles are asymmetric.

title: Minimum Cable Diameter for Required FOS
learningObjectives: Determine required cable area and diameter from tension and allowable stress.
student: If the cable material has failure normal stress σfail = {{sigma_fail}} MPa and the required factor of safety is {{FOS_req}}, determine the minimum required diameter of each cable.
instructor: The allowable stress is σallow = σfail/FOSreq = {{sigma_fail}}/{{FOS_req}} = {{cable_allowable_stress_MPa}} MPa. Required area is Areq = T/σallow. Therefore AAB,req = {{cable_A_AB_req_mm2}} mm2, dAB,min = {{cable_d_AB_min_mm}} mm; ABC,req = {{cable_A_BC_req_mm2}} mm2, dBC,min = {{cable_d_BC_min_mm}} mm.
gradingNotes: Because MPa = N/mm2, using T in N gives area in mm2 and diameter in mm.

title: Strength FOS Check for Selected Diameters
learningObjectives: Compute cable stress and FOS for selected cable diameters.
student: Now suppose cable AB has diameter dAB = {{d_AB}} mm and cable BC has diameter dBC = {{d_BC}} mm. Determine the normal stress and factor of safety in each cable.
instructor: AAB = π({{d_AB}})2/4 = {{cable_A_AB_mm2}} mm2, so σAB = TAB/AAB = {{cable_sigma_AB_MPa}} MPa and FOSAB = {{sigma_fail}}/{{cable_sigma_AB_MPa}} = {{cable_FOS_AB}}. ABC = π({{d_BC}})2/4 = {{cable_A_BC_mm2}} mm2, so σBC = TBC/ABC = {{cable_sigma_BC_MPa}} MPa and FOSBC = {{sigma_fail}}/{{cable_sigma_BC_MPa}} = {{cable_FOS_BC}}. The governing selected-diameter FOS is {{cable_governing_fos}} in {{cable_governing_fos_member}}.

title: Strength-Based Modification
learningObjectives: Propose mechanics-based changes when a factor of safety requirement is not met.
student: If either cable does not meet the required factor of safety, identify a mechanics-based modification that would increase the factor of safety.
instructor: Possible modifications include increasing the diameter of the governing cable, selecting a cable material with larger failure stress, reducing the supported mass, or changing the cable geometry to reduce the tension in the governing cable. For this numerical case, {{cable_design_recommendation}}.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a limited engineering recommendation based on cable strength and missing connector checks.
student: Using the mechanics results, make a limited engineering recommendation for the suspended equipment support. Include connector or anchor checks that would be needed before final service approval.
instructor: The governing load case is the static weight of the {{m}} kg equipment pod, W = {{cable_weight_N}} N. Cable {{cable_governing_tension_member}} carries the larger tension. For the minimum-diameter design, use dAB ≥ {{cable_d_AB_min_mm}} mm and dBC ≥ {{cable_d_BC_min_mm}} mm before rounding up to standard cable sizes. For dAB = {{d_AB}} mm and dBC = {{d_BC}} mm, the selected-diameter check gives FOSAB = {{cable_FOS_AB}} and FOSBC = {{cable_FOS_BC}}; therefore, {{cable_design_recommendation}}. Final service acceptance still requires separate verification of wall anchors, brackets, shackles, pins, fatigue if cyclic loading exists, and installation quality.
gradingNotes: The recommendation should return to the real support system without claiming connector or anchor safety from cable stress alone.
